subject: Social Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 10 periods = 450 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 7h 30min

periods.activity_title: What Goes Into Making Something? Mapping Inputs at Pause Point

time_bands.activity: Pose this question to the class: 'Ratna wants to open a small restaurant on the outskirts of the city — what does she actually need before she can serve her first meal?' Students spend a quick individual list-making exercise writing every requirement they can think of. Call on four or five students and record responses on the board without categorising yet, letting the raw variety accumulate.

Read through the Pause Point scenario together, pausing at each input Ratna must organise — choosing a location, arranging money, hiring staff, buying ingredients, planning menus. Ask students to revisit their lists and mark which items match Ratna's and which new ones they had missed. Then pose: 'Can Ratna replace any one of these inputs and still run the restaurant?' — let three or four students argue yes or no and justify, directing the class toward the idea that inputs are interdependent.

Students individually complete the input-mapping worksheet: in the left column they list six economic activities visible in their own locality (e.g., a tea stall, a tailor, an auto-repair garage); in the right column they write at least two inputs each activity requires. Pairs then compare and discuss any activity where they identified different inputs for the same business, explaining their reasoning to each other.

Bring the class back together. Ask: 'What broad types or families of inputs appeared across all the businesses on your lists?' Receive answers and hint that economists have a systematic way of classifying these — four named categories plus technology — which the chapter will explore section by section. Record the four words 'land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship' on the board and tell students these are the chapter's central organising framework, to be unpacked in coming units.

periods.section_context: Ratna's Pause Point restaurant, locality economic activity inputs survey
periods.teacher_notes: Open the chapter by anchoring it in the students' own locality so that abstract economic vocabulary grows from a familiar ground. A common confusion at this stage is treating 'ingredients' or 'raw materials' as a separate category rather than recognising them as one form of a broader 'land/natural resources' input — hold this tension rather than resolving it prematurely, as the next unit addresses it directly. Encourage students to name specific local businesses, not generic ones, so the locality survey feels like genuine observation rather than a textbook exercise.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students collect and organise information about economic institutions in their locality and explain their significance.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can collect and classify input information from multiple local economic activities to identify patterns in how businesses are organised.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify the range of inputs any production activity requires and explain why no single input is sufficient on its own.

periods.activity_title: Beyond Dirt: What Economists Mean by 'Land'

time_bands.activity: Write the word 'land' on the board and ask students to call out what it means to them — expect responses like 'soil', 'a plot', 'farming land'. Then ask: 'If a bottled-water company uses groundwater, does it use land? If a solar farm uses sunlight, does it use land?' Let three or four students react. This surfaces the mismatch between everyday and economic uses of the word and sets up the section's definitional expansion.

Work through the section's full list of natural resources — soil, forests, water, air, sunlight, minerals, oil, and natural gas — asking for one real Indian business that depends on each. For each example, ask: 'Does this business purchase land outright, or does it pay rent to use it for a period of time?' (e.g., a miner leasing extraction rights vs. a farmer owning fields). Record a two-column table on the board: 'Purchased' vs. 'Rented access', filling in student examples. This builds the economic distinction between owning and accessing land as a factor.

Students return to the locality input-mapping worksheet they built in the introductory unit. Using one colour of sticky note they label every item on their list that now qualifies as 'land' under the economic definition, and a second colour for items they initially called 'land' but now realise are something else. Each student shares one reclassification with a partner and explains the reasoning. Bring two or three examples to the whole class.

Close with the supply-geography question: 'Natural resources are not spread evenly across India — coal is in Jharkhand, fish in coastal states, oil in Gujarat and Assam. How might that uneven distribution affect a business that needs one of these resources?' Students write a three-sentence response in their notebooks. Collect one sentence from four students to close the discussion, setting up the idea that resource geography shapes production decisions.

periods.section_context: Soil, forests, water, sunlight, minerals, oil, rent vs. purchase of land
periods.teacher_notes: Having mapped inputs for local businesses, students are ready to scrutinise one category — land — in depth. The most persistent confusion is conflating physical land (a plot) with the economist's meaning (all natural resources); the sticky-note reclassification makes that distinction tactile and personal. The closing geography prompt intentionally plants an idea that the 'How are the Factors Connected?' section develops later, so do not resolve the distribution question here — let it sit as an open question.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply the economist's definition of land to classify natural resource inputs across varied production contexts.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students recognise the geographic distribution of resources and explain its implications for production.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how the uneven geographic distribution of natural resources influences where and how production is organised.

periods.activity_title: Labour, Human Capital, and the Skills That Develop It
periods.section_anchor: Labour (human resources) / Facilitators of human capital
materials: Three-column analysis table (printed or drawn in notebook)

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'A carpenter and a civil engineer both use their hands and minds at work — what, if anything, makes their contributions economically different?' Take four or five responses, then introduce the section's key distinction: labour is physical and mental effort (carpenters, farmers, construction workers, teachers, doctors); human capital is the quality of that effort — the specialised skills, knowledge, and expertise behind it. Write both terms on the board with a one-line definition each and have students copy them.

Move to the three facilitators that build human capital. For Education and Training: present the civil engineering student example — classroom design principles plus hands-on site observation. Ask: 'Which part is education and which is training? Could either alone produce a competent engineer?' For Healthcare: pose the reflective question from the section — 'How does healthcare infrastructure develop human capital?' — and ask students to reason through the chain: health → school attendance → learning → productivity. For Social and Cultural Influences: explain the Japanese concept of kaizen (continuous improvement, applied since the mid-1940s) and the German work ethic (punctuality, attention to detail, quality focus). Ask: 'Can a culture be an economic resource? How?' Students respond in pairs before sharing with the class.

Students complete a three-column table in their notebooks: Column 1 — Facilitator (Education/Training, Healthcare, Culture); Column 2 — How it builds human capital (in their own words, one sentence each); Column 3 — One example from India or their locality where this facilitator is strong or weak. Walk the room, prompting students who leave Column 3 blank to think of a government school, a local health centre, or a workplace norm they have observed.

Whole-class share: one student reads their Column 3 entry for each facilitator. After each, ask the class: 'Does anyone have a contrasting example — where the same facilitator fails?' Close by asking students to name one thing that would need to change in their locality for human capital to improve, connecting the facilitator framework to a real place.

periods.section_context: Labour vs. human capital distinction; education, healthcare, kaizen, German work ethic
periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently treat labour and human capital as synonyms — the civil engineer vs. carpenter contrast is the section's own tool for pulling them apart, so return to it whenever a student conflates the two. The kaizen and German work ethic examples risk feeling distant; anchoring them to a student's own locality example (Column 3) brings the facilitator logic home. The workplace culture survey suggested in the chapter works well as a prompt for Column 3 rather than a separate homework task, keeping the unit self-contained.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can distinguish between labour and human capital and explain how education, healthcare, and cultural values develop the quality of human resources.

periods.activity_title: Demographic Dividend or Missed Opportunity? India's Human Capital Challenge
materials: Data card (teacher-prepared, one per pair): Adult Literacy Rate 85% male / 70% female, 65% of Indians below 35

time_bands.activity: Distribute the data card and give pairs two minutes to read it silently. Then ask: 'What do these two statistics — literacy rates and age distribution — have to do with each other?' Take four responses without confirming or denying. This surfaces initial reasoning about the connection between education and the demographic dividend before the section frames it explicitly.

Work through the section with the class. Define demographic dividend: the economic benefit a country gains when it has a large, young, working population with fewer dependants, drawing on the Economic Survey of India 2024 figure that 65% of Indians are below 35. Then present the literacy data: Adult Literacy Rate in India as of 2023 stands at 85% for males and 70% for females (World Bank estimates). Pose the analytical question: 'If 65% of Indians are young and potentially productive, but literacy rates still show a gender gap, what does that mean for whether India actually realises its demographic dividend?' Students discuss in pairs for three minutes, then share two or three responses.

Present the Think About It scenario from the chapter: a child who loses two years of schooling due to illness or family circumstances. Students write a structured response addressing three questions in their notebooks: (1) What skills does that child likely miss? (2) How might this affect their future earning capacity? (3) What would need to happen — at the family, community, or government level — to recover those two years? After writing, pairs compare and note where their answers differ.

Class discussion: 'India has a potential demographic dividend, but it comes with conditions. What are those conditions?' Build a list on the board — quality education, health access, training, skilling — using students' language. Close by asking: 'Who is responsible for creating these conditions — individuals, families, businesses, or governments?' Encourage multiple positions; do not resolve the debate, as the Responsibilities section will return to it.

periods.section_context: Demographic dividend, literacy gender gap, schooling loss, quality education and health conditions
periods.teacher_notes: Having built the concept of human capital and its facilitators, students now encounter the gap between potential and reality in India's specific context. A common confusion is treating the demographic dividend as automatic — students need to see that it is conditional on quality human capital development, not guaranteed by a young population alone. The gender literacy gap (85% vs. 70%) often prompts rich discussion about unequal access; let that discussion develop before moving to the structural conditions.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the conditions required to convert a young population into an economic asset by connecting literacy data to the demographic dividend concept.

periods.activity_title: Ancient Craft, Living Knowledge: India's Skill Heritage
materials: Source excerpt card (teacher-prepared): one short description of stitched shipbuilding from the chapter summary

time_bands.activity: Ask the class: 'What is the oldest technology you have ever used or seen used — something that was invented long before you were born but still works today?' Take five or six responses. Then ask: 'Could knowledge this old count as a form of human capital — something that contributes to production?' This question bridges the earlier human capital discussion to the section's claim that India's ancient skill heritage is economically significant.

Present the section's two main pillars. First: the shilpa shastras — texts containing detailed design guidelines for sculptures, paintings, buildings, wooden items, and jewellery — passed from generation to generation. Explain the chapter's framing: for ancient Indians, work was an offering requiring devotion, blending kalā (art) and vidyā (knowledge); tools were worshipped, a tradition continuing as Vishwakarma Puja or Ayudha Puja. Second: distribute the source excerpt card on stitched shipbuilding — a technique over 2,000 years old in which wooden planks were stitched using cords rather than nails, making ships flexible and suited to Indian Ocean navigation. Ask: 'What problem was this technique solving? What does it tell us about the level of material knowledge ancient Indian craftspeople possessed?'

Source analysis in pairs: students read the stitched shipbuilding excerpt and answer three structured questions — (1) What physical property did the stitching technique give the ship, and why did that matter for Indian Ocean sailing? (2) What does the existence of the shilpa shastras suggest about how knowledge was organised and preserved in ancient India? (3) The chapter says these indigenous techniques have declined — list two reasons why that might have happened. Pairs write brief answers; circulate and prompt with follow-up questions.

Whole-class debrief. Take one answer to each question from different pairs. Then ask: 'How does documenting and teaching these techniques — in schools, apprenticeships, or museums — relate to developing human capital today?' Close by inviting students to name one traditional technique from their own region they know about or have seen, connecting the chapter's national examples to local heritage.

periods.section_context: Shilpa shastras, kalā and vidyā, Vishwakarma Puja, stitched shipbuilding and Indian Ocean trade
periods.teacher_notes: Having examined modern facilitators and challenges of human capital, students now encounter a historical dimension: India's own deep tradition of codified, transmitted skill. A frequent confusion is treating ancient techniques as mere historical curiosities rather than as evidence of sophisticated knowledge systems — the stitched shipbuilding example is particularly useful because it demonstrates a deliberate engineering choice, not primitive limitation. The link to Vishwakarma and Ayudha Puja grounds an abstract concept in a cultural practice many students may recognise from their own experience.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students know and appreciate India's historical contributions to knowledge, skill, and cultural heritage.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret evidence from ancient Indian skill traditions to explain how knowledge was organised, transmitted, and applied in production.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect ancient Indian skill heritage to the broader concept of human capital and explain its contribution to historical production and trade.

periods.activity_title: Capital: What It Is, Where It Comes From, and How Businesses Access It
materials: Capital source decision-tree worksheet (teacher-prepared, one per student)

time_bands.activity: Return to Ratna's restaurant, Pause Point. Ask: 'Ratna has chosen her location, hired a cook, and sourced her vegetables — but she still needs to lease the space, buy furniture, and purchase kitchen equipment. What is she missing, and where might she get it?' Take four or five responses. Students will likely say 'money', 'a loan', 'savings'. Record these on the board — they are the raw material for the section's definition and source framework.

Define capital from the section: monetary resources AND durable human-made assets — machinery, tools, equipment, vehicles, computers, shops, factories, office buildings — used for day-to-day operations. Clarify: money itself is capital only when used for production, not for consumption. Then work through the three sources of capital: personal savings and family/friends (the entrepreneur's first recourse); bank loans (when personal funds are insufficient); and the stock market (large companies raising public money by selling shares and offering dividends). For each source, ask: 'What type of business or what stage of growth would typically use this source? What are the risks?' Build a three-row table on the board.

Students complete the capital source decision-tree worksheet: given four business scenarios of increasing scale (a street food cart, a tailor's shop, a regional textile mill, a national electronics company), they identify the most likely capital sources and give one reason for each choice. Circulate; prompt students who default to 'bank loan' for every scenario by asking them to think about what a bank requires before lending.

Debrief the worksheet using the local factory prompt from the chapter: 'Think of a factory or large business in your area — a rice mill, a brick kiln, a workshop. Estimate what physical capital it needs and where the owner might have obtained the starting money.' Two or three students share their estimates and reasoning. Close by asking: 'Why is access to capital a challenge for small entrepreneurs but less so for large companies?' — leaving this as a question the Entrepreneurship unit will deepen.

periods.section_context: Capital as money plus durable assets; personal savings, bank loans, stock market shares and dividends
periods.teacher_notes: Having established land and labour as factors, students now examine capital — the factor most often conflated with 'money' alone. The distinction between money and durable productive assets (machinery, buildings) is the section's key conceptual move; the decision-tree worksheet forces students to apply it rather than repeat it. The stock market and dividends may be unfamiliar vocabulary — a brief, concrete explanation ('the company sells a small ownership share to many people, who receive a portion of profits') is sufficient without turning the unit into a finance lesson.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can classify the components of capital and match the appropriate source of capital to different scales and types of production.

periods.activity_title: The Entrepreneur's Role: Risk, Innovation, and Social Impact
materials: J.R.D. Tata profile card (teacher-prepared from chapter summary)
Entrepreneurship analysis grid (one per student, teacher-prepared)

time_bands.activity: Ask the class: 'We now have land, labour, and capital as factors of production. Is there a missing ingredient — something that decides how all three get combined, what gets made, and who bears the risk if it fails?' Take responses. Introduce entrepreneurship as the factor that identifies a problem, develops an innovative solution, organises the other factors, makes key decisions, takes risks, and contributes to society's welfare. Write the five defining functions on the board.

Distribute the J.R.D. Tata profile card and read it together: born 1904, led the Tata Group, founded Tata Airlines in 1932 (later Air India — India's first airline), expanded into steel, cars, power, and chemicals, known for workers' welfare, awarded the Bharat Ratna in 1992. Students work individually to complete the entrepreneurship analysis grid: for each of the five functions written on the board (identify problem, innovate, organise factors, take risks, contribute to society) they write one specific piece of evidence from J.R.D. Tata's profile. Circulate and prompt: 'What problem did a domestic airline solve in 1932? What risk did starting it involve?'

Introduce startups: an entrepreneurial venture with limited resources aiming at rapid growth through technology. Ask: 'How does a startup's relationship to risk differ from an established company like Tata?' Then pose the Think About It question from the chapter: 'What motivates entrepreneurs beyond profit — what did J.R.D. Tata's care for workers' welfare tell us about motivations other than money?' Small groups of three discuss for four minutes and share one insight each.

Students choose one local business they know — a shop, a service provider, a small manufacturer — and apply the entrepreneurship grid to it: which of the five functions does the owner perform? Write four sentences in their notebooks. Take three examples from the room. Close with: 'Every business, however small, has someone performing the entrepreneurship function — the difference is scale and formality.' Link to the upcoming unit by noting that technology increasingly shapes how entrepreneurs combine the other factors.

periods.section_context: Entrepreneur functions, J.R.D. Tata and Tata Airlines 1932, Bharat Ratna 1992, startups
periods.teacher_notes: Having established capital, students now encounter the factor that organises all the others — entrepreneurship. A common confusion is treating entrepreneurship as synonymous with business ownership; the five-function grid forces students to see it as a set of active economic operations, not a title. J.R.D. Tata's care for workers' welfare is the chapter's own evidence that entrepreneurship carries social dimensions alongside profit-seeking — this point is worth dwelling on, as it connects forward to the Responsibilities section.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can apply the defining functions of entrepreneurship to real business profiles and explain how entrepreneurs create economic and social value.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students collect and organise information about economic institutions and explain their significance.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse the role of a major economic institution and a local business using the same entrepreneurship framework to compare scale and function.

periods.activity_title: Technology as Enabler: From Pulleys to SWAYAM
materials: Technology impact analysis table (drawn in notebook)

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 'Technology is the application of scientific knowledge to production-related activities.' Ask: 'Is a pulley technology? Is a wheelbarrow? Is UPI? Is a GPS tracker on a delivery van?' Take rapid responses to establish that technology spans ancient tools and modern digital systems. Then ask: 'What do all of these have in common as a factor of production?' — directing students toward the idea that technology enables producers to do more with the same or fewer other inputs.

Work through the section's modern examples. UPI payments: how does enabling instant digital payments change a small vendor's ability to do business? GPS for logistics: how does knowing a truck's location in real time reduce waste and speed delivery? Drones for crop management: how does aerial monitoring reduce labour and chemicals needed? For each, ask students to name which other factor of production the technology reduces the need for or makes more effective. Record a three-column table on the board: Technology | Factor it enables | Factor it reduces reliance on.

Shift to the knowledge-access dimension. Explain SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds): free Massive Open Online Courses for learners from Grade 9 upwards, covering subjects such as robotics, aquaculture, and textile printing. Explain the National Career Service portal: connects job seekers to opportunities across sectors. Ask: 'How does eliminating geographical barriers to education and employment change the human capital equation?' Students construct a four-row technology impact table in their notebooks, one row each for: SWAYAM, National Career Service portal, drones, GPS — with columns for 'What it enables' and 'Who benefits most'.

Students share one row from their tables. Then pose the community question from the section: 'Name one technological advancement that has changed your community in the last ten years — for better or for worse — and explain the change.' Take five or six responses spanning digital and physical technologies. Close by noting that the next unit examines how all five factors — including technology — work together and sometimes compete within a single production process.

periods.section_context: UPI, GPS logistics, drones, SWAYAM platform, National Career Service portal, pulleys
periods.teacher_notes: Having defined entrepreneurship as the factor that organises others, students now encounter technology as a cross-cutting enabler that changes the proportions in which the other factors are combined. Students often see technology as exclusively digital and modern; the pulley and wheelbarrow examples from the section correct this and also prevent students from dismissing their own community's older technologies as irrelevant. SWAYAM and the National Career Service portal are government institutional examples that connect directly to the C-4.1 competency's concern with institutions and their societal significance.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain how technology changes the combination of factors in production and assess its impact on access to knowledge and employment.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students collect and organise information about economic institutions and explain their significance.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can describe government technology platforms such as SWAYAM and the National Career Service portal and explain their significance for human capital development.

periods.activity_title: Five Factors, One Product: Tracing the Mobile Phone Supply Chain
materials: Mobile phone assembly case study card (teacher-prepared from chapter summary)

time_bands.activity: Hold up a mobile phone (or draw one on the board) and ask: 'Before this phone reached your hand, how many different factors of production were involved in making it?' Take four or five initial responses. Then ask: 'Is mobile phone manufacturing labour-intensive or capital-intensive — or both?' Surface the two terms from the section: labour-intensive (agriculture, construction, handicrafts, relying more on human effort) vs. capital-intensive (semiconductor chips, satellites, requiring more machinery and specialised equipment). Students place the mobile phone on a spectrum between the two and justify their placement.

Distribute the mobile phone assembly case study card. India is the world's second-largest mobile phone manufacturer as of 2025. Work through the case with the class, tracing each factor at each stage: Land (minerals like lithium and silicon from mines); Labour (assembly workers, engineers, quality inspectors); Capital (factories, machines, logistics vehicles); Entrepreneurship (company decisions about design, market, and risk); Technology (precision robotics, GPS tracking of parts, digital supply chain management). Record a five-row table on the board with one example per factor.

Pairs complete a cause-effect mapping grid for the supply chain disruption scenario: during the COVID-19 pandemic, global supply chains for electronic components broke down. Students map — for three factors (Land/resources, Labour, Technology/Capital) — what the disruption was and what production effect it caused. They then answer: 'The chapter says over-reliance on distant sources can disrupt the supply chain. What strategy might a manufacturer adopt to reduce this risk?' Write two sentences per factor and one recommendation.

Debrief the grid as a class. Take answers from three pairs. Then pose the transformation question from the section: '3-D printing could help revive dying textile art forms — how does this relate to the ancient skill heritage covered earlier in the chapter?' This question connects two sections of the chapter analytically. Close by asking students to state one factor interdependency they found most surprising in the mobile phone case.

periods.section_context: Labour-intensive vs. capital-intensive production, mobile phone assembly India, supply chain COVID-19 disruption
periods.teacher_notes: Having studied each factor individually, students now confront their interdependence through a concrete, current case — India's mobile phone manufacturing industry. The supply chain disruption during the COVID-19 pandemic is the section's own analytical anchor for showing that factor interdependence creates vulnerability; resist the temptation to resolve the disruption discussion with a tidy policy answer, as the complexity itself is the lesson. The 3-D printing and textile arts connection rewards students who engaged with the ancient skill heritage unit and makes the chapter's internal coherence visible.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the contribution of all five factors of production through a single supply chain and analyse the consequences when any factor is disrupted.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students recognise the geographic distribution of resources and explain its implications for production.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can analyse how the geographic dispersal of inputs across a supply chain creates both productive capacity and vulnerability to disruption.

periods.activity_title: Who Is Responsible? Producers, Workers, and the Environment
materials: Responsibility analysis worksheet (teacher-prepared, one per student)

time_bands.activity: Ask: 'If a factory owner uses a river to dispose of waste chemicals, who is harmed? Who is responsible? And if the law says nothing about it, does responsibility still exist?' Take five responses, deliberately including students who say 'no legal obligation, no responsibility' alongside those who argue otherwise. This surfaces the normative terrain the section navigates — that production carries obligations beyond profit, whether or not they are mandated.

Work through the three domains of responsibility the section identifies. Environmental: the Tamil Nadu leather factory example — tanneries that pollute rivers and soil, and improperly recycled smartphones releasing harmful substances. Ask: 'What specific actions could each of these producers take to reduce harm?' Students name concrete steps (waste treatment, certified recycling). Workers: the three areas the section identifies — fair compensation and working conditions; skill development and training; upholding workplace rights and protections against discrimination. For each, ask students to give one example of what failing this responsibility looks like. CSR: India was the first country in the world to enact a CSR law, in 2014, mandating companies to spend 2% of their average three-year profits on CSR activities. Ask: 'Why might a government need to mandate responsibility rather than relying on voluntary action?'

Students complete the responsibility analysis worksheet: given two brief scenarios — (A) a garment factory that sub-contracts to home workers paid below minimum wage with no training; (B) a chemical plant that funds a local school but discharges untreated effluent into a stream — they identify which responsibility domains are violated, which are met, and propose two specific corrective actions for each scenario. Pairs compare their proposed actions and note where they agree or disagree.

Whole-class discussion: 'Should the 2% CSR mandate be increased, kept the same, or removed — and who should decide?' Students argue a position in two sentences. Take four or five positions and let brief counter-arguments follow. Close by returning to the chapter's opening: 'Ratna at Pause Point uses land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship — what responsibilities does she have toward each factor, even as a small business owner?' This closes the chapter on the same narrative it opened with, completing the conceptual arc.

periods.section_context: Tamil Nadu leather factories, smartphone recycling, CSR law 2014, worker rights and fair compensation
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter's concluding section turns from description to normative analysis — students must evaluate obligations, not merely describe factors. The Tamil Nadu leather factory and smartphone recycling examples are the section's own evidence of real harm; using them grounds the discussion in documented cases rather than hypothetical ones. India's 2014 CSR law as a global first is a point of factual pride that can motivate engagement, but push students to also think critically about whether a mandate is as effective as genuine ethical commitment — the chapter itself does not resolve this tension.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the responsibility of producers and institutions to use resources sustainably and treat workers fairly.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate producer responsibilities toward the environment and workers and assess the role of legal mechanisms such as CSR in enforcing those responsibilities.

competency_edges.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can connect each factor of production to the responsibilities it generates and explain why sustainable and fair use of factors matters for society.

competency.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the range of inputs any production activity requires and explain why no single input is sufficient on its own.
assessment_items.question_text: Ratna wants to open a small restaurant, Pause Point. She has found a good location, hired a cook, and sourced her vegetables. Which statement best explains why she still cannot begin operations?

options.label: A
options.text: She has not yet combined all the necessary factors of production — money to lease the space and buy equipment is still missing.

options.label: B
options.text: She needs to register her restaurant with the government before she can hire any staff.

options.label: C
options.text: Labour is the most important factor, so hiring more cooks will resolve any remaining gap.

options.label: D
options.text: Natural resources are automatically provided by the government to new small businesses.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may respond orally or by pointing to the option if writing is a barrier.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses a legal/administrative requirement with an economic factor of production — suggests the student is thinking about procedural steps rather than the factors framework.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a misconception that one factor (labour) can substitute for all others — indicates the student has not grasped factor interdependence.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Suggests a confusion between public goods and factors of production — the student may be conflating government services with the economic concept of land or capital.

competency.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply the economist's definition of land to classify natural resource inputs across varied production contexts.
assessment_items.question_text: A solar energy company generates electricity using sunlight collected over a large open area. A bottled-water company extracts groundwater from beneath farmland. In economics, both sunlight and groundwater are classified as the same factor of production. What is that factor, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Capital, because both require machinery and equipment to harness and process.

options.label: B
options.text: Land, because in economics 'land' includes all natural resources — soil, water, sunlight, minerals, and more — not only physical ground.

options.label: C
options.text: Technology, because both companies use scientific methods to convert natural phenomena into usable energy or water.

options.label: D
options.text: Labour, because workers are needed to operate the equipment that collects sunlight and extracts groundwater.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses the machinery used to harness a natural resource (capital) with the resource itself — the student sees the equipment rather than the input.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates the method of accessing a natural resource (technology) with the resource category — indicates the student is classifying by process rather than by what is being used.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reduces classification to the presence of workers rather than to the nature of the input — suggests the student defaults to labour as a catch-all.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Labour (human resources) / Facilitators of human capital
assessment_items.question_text: A civil engineering student attends classroom lectures on structural design and also visits construction sites to observe work in progress. Explain the difference between labour and human capital using this student as your example. Then identify two facilitators that are building this student's human capital and explain how each one works.
expected_elements: A clear distinction between labour (physical and mental effort in production) and human capital (the quality, skill, and expertise behind that effort).
Identification of education as one facilitator — explaining how classroom instruction gives the student the knowledge base needed to perform specialised engineering work.
Identification of training as a second facilitator — explaining how site observation develops practical, applied competence that complements formal study.
The explanation connects the facilitator directly to an improvement in the quality of the student's future labour, not merely to the student gaining knowledge.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a simple two-column layout (labour / human capital) if a prose response is difficult to organise.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the conditions required to convert a young population into an economic asset by connecting literacy data to the demographic dividend concept.
assessment_items.question_text: According to the Economic Survey of India 2024, 65 per cent of Indians are below the age of 35. According to World Bank estimates for 2023, the Adult Literacy Rate in India is 85 per cent for males and 70 per cent for females. Using these figures and the concept of demographic dividend, evaluate whether India is currently in a strong position to convert its young population into an economic advantage. Your response must take a clear position and support it with reasoning from the data and the conditions the chapter identifies.
look_for: A clear, stated position — either that India is well-placed, not yet well-placed, or partially placed — with a reason given for the stance.
Accurate use of 'demographic dividend' as the economic benefit of a large, young, working population with fewer dependants, not merely a synonym for 'many young people'.
Engagement with the gender literacy gap (85% male vs. 70% female) as evidence that human capital development is uneven, affecting the quality of the potential workforce.
Identification of at least two specific conditions — quality education, health access, training, or skilling — that the chapter says must be met for the dividend to be realised.
A reasoned judgement that goes beyond restating facts — the student shows they can weigh the positive (large young population) against the gap evidence (literacy disparity) to reach a conclusion.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult may use a structured outline: Position → Evidence 1 → Evidence 2 → Condition needed → Conclusion.

competency.competency_text: Students explain the key elements of production and their impact on individual life and society.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the contribution of all five factors of production through a single supply chain and analyse the consequences when any factor is disrupted.
assessment_items.task: India is the world's second-largest mobile phone manufacturer as of 2025. During the COVID-19 pandemic, global supply chains for electronic components broke down, disrupting production severely. Using the five factors of production — land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship, and technology — create a cause-effect map that shows: (a) how each factor contributes to mobile phone assembly in normal times, and (b) what happened to production when supply chains were disrupted. Then add one recommendation for how manufacturers could reduce their vulnerability to a similar disruption in the future.
assessment_items.scaffold: Your cause-effect map should have two columns: 'Normal Production' and 'Disruption Effect'. Add one row for each of the five factors. In the 'Normal Production' column, write one specific way that factor contributes to making a mobile phone. In the 'Disruption Effect' column, write what went wrong with that factor during the COVID-19 supply chain crisis. Below the table, write 2–3 sentences explaining your recommendation and which factor(s) it protects.
format_of_output: A two-column, five-row cause-effect map (hand-drawn table is acceptable)
2–3 sentences of written recommendation below the table
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may label their table in a home language alongside English if it helps them articulate their reasoning. Oral explanation of the recommendation to the teacher is an acceptable alternative to written sentences.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: This task demonstrates whether students can hold all five factors simultaneously in mind, apply each to a real production case, and then reason about systemic vulnerability — moving from description to analysis and finally to a policy-level recommendation. It directly realises the LO's demand to trace factor contributions through a supply chain and analyse disruption consequences.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The two-column structure prevents students from writing about factors in isolation — the disruption column forces them to connect normal function to what breaks down. The recommendation prompt requires them to synthesise across multiple factors rather than treating disruption as a simple single-factor problem.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: each cell names a specific contribution or specific disruption (e.g., 'semiconductor minerals from overseas mines — supply cut off when borders closed'); the recommendation targets a structural vulnerability (e.g., building domestic supply for key minerals) rather than a generic fix ('be prepared'). Weak responses: cells are vague ('land provides materials'; 'disruption affected production'); recommendation is a platitude without identifying which factor it addresses.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: A cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the LO itself requires students to trace factor contributions and analyse disruption consequences — a map externalises that causal chain in a form the teacher can read and assess in a single sitting. The teacher may substitute any other format from the permitted menu.

competency.competency_text: Students explain the responsibility of producers and institutions to use resources sustainably and treat workers fairly.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate producer responsibilities toward the environment and workers and assess the role of legal mechanisms such as CSR in enforcing those responsibilities.
assessment_items.question_text: A leather factory in Tamil Nadu discharges untreated chemical waste into a nearby river, harming local fish populations and the health of residents downstream. The factory owner argues that no law currently prohibits this specific type of discharge. Which response best evaluates the owner's argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The owner is correct — if no specific law prohibits the discharge, there is no responsibility, and the factory may continue as before.

options.label: B
options.text: The owner's argument is too narrow — producers have a responsibility to avoid pollution and protect natural resources regardless of whether a specific prohibition exists, because future generations also depend on those resources.

options.label: C
options.text: The owner should apply for a government exemption — once approved, all environmental damage caused by the factory becomes the government's legal responsibility.

options.label: D
options.text: The problem lies only with the workers — it is their duty to refuse to operate equipment that causes environmental harm.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a 'legal positivism' misconception — the student conflates legal compliance with the full scope of responsibility, missing the chapter's argument that producers have obligations beyond what law mandates.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests a confusion about how government exemptions work and who bears responsibility — the student has not understood that CSR and producer responsibility cannot be transferred to the state through a permit.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Mislocates responsibility at the worker level rather than the producer level — the student may have understood that workers have protections but missed that environmental responsibility rests with the business owner or operator.

competency.competency_text: Students explain the responsibility of producers and institutions to use resources sustainably and treat workers fairly.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate producer responsibilities toward the environment and workers and assess the role of legal mechanisms such as CSR in enforcing those responsibilities.
assessment_items.question_text: India was the first country in the world to enact a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) law, in 2014, requiring companies above a certain size to spend 2 per cent of their average three-year profits on social and environmental activities. A student argues: 'If companies were truly responsible, this law would not be needed.' Which of the following best evaluates this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is entirely wrong — the CSR law proves that all Indian companies are irresponsible and must be forced to act.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is entirely right — a truly responsible company would spend far more than 2 per cent without any legal compulsion.

options.label: C
options.text: The student raises a valid tension — legal mandates can guarantee a minimum level of social investment but may not substitute for the deeper ethical commitment the chapter describes as genuine producer responsibility.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is irrelevant — CSR spending decisions are purely financial and have nothing to do with ethics or responsibility.

assessment_items.inclusivity: The teacher may read the options aloud for students who benefit from auditory processing.

what_each_option_reveals.A: An overcorrection — the student dismisses the student's argument entirely by converting it into a sweeping condemnation of all companies, missing the nuance that the law and voluntary ethics can coexist.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Accepts the argument uncritically without recognising that legal floors can have value even alongside voluntary action — the student conflates the question of sufficiency with the question of necessity.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fails to recognise that CSR is explicitly a responsibility mechanism, not merely a financial decision — suggests the student has not engaged with the chapter's framing of CSR as an ethical and legal instrument.

competency.competency_text: Students explain the responsibility of producers and institutions to use resources sustainably and treat workers fairly.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate producer responsibilities toward the environment and workers and assess the role of legal mechanisms such as CSR in enforcing those responsibilities.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter identifies three areas in which producers are responsible toward their workers: fair compensation and working conditions; skill development and training; and upholding workplace rights and protections against discrimination. A garment factory pays its workers below the minimum wage, provides no training, and dismisses workers who raise safety concerns. Identify which responsibilities this factory is failing in each of the three areas and explain, for any one area, what the factory would need to do differently to meet its responsibility.
expected_elements: Identification of fair compensation failure — workers paid below minimum wage violates the responsibility for fair pay and acceptable working conditions.
Identification of skill development failure — no training provided means the factory is not investing in workers' capacity to perform or advance.
Identification of workplace rights failure — dismissing workers who raise safety concerns violates protections against retaliation and suppresses rights.

For one area chosen: a specific, actionable corrective step (e.g., 'the factory should set wages at or above the legal minimum and review them regularly' or 'establish a formal safety complaint channel with non-retaliation guarantees').
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may number their three identifications (1, 2, 3) and then write the corrective explanation as a fourth point if a paragraph structure is difficult.

competency.competency_text: Students collect and organise information about economic institutions and explain their significance.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can collect and classify input information from multiple local economic activities to identify patterns in how businesses are organised.

options.label: A
options.text: All four businesses rely primarily on a single factor of production, which is labour.

options.label: B
options.text: The auto-repair garage and the tailor's shop both combine physical skill (labour) with tools and equipment (capital), showing that even small local businesses combine multiple factors.

options.label: C
options.text: Only the restaurant requires entrepreneurship because it is the only business that involves risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Natural resources (land) are not involved in any of these four businesses because none of them involves farming or mining.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Business | Key inputs listed by a student surveyor
Small restaurant | Vegetables and spices (natural resources), cooking equipment (capital), cooks and servers (labour), space/building (land/capital)
Tailor's shop | Fabric (natural resources), sewing machines (capital), tailoring skill (labour), shop space (land/capital)
Auto-repair garage | Metal parts (natural resources/capital), tools and lifts (capital), mechanical skill (labour), garage space (land/capital)
Tea stall | Tea leaves and milk (natural resources), gas stove and kettle (capital), stall operator (labour), roadside space (land)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals that the student is not reading the table carefully — all four businesses show capital inputs listed alongside labour, so the claim that labour is the sole factor contradicts the data.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reflects a misconception that entrepreneurship belongs only to larger or riskier businesses — the student has not understood that every business owner exercises the entrepreneurship function.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Shows a confusion between the everyday meaning of 'land' (farming/mining) and the economist's definition (all natural resources) — vegetables, tea leaves, fabric, and metal parts are all land inputs in the economic sense.

competency.competency_text: Students collect and organise information about economic institutions and explain their significance.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse the role of a major economic institution and a local business using the same entrepreneurship framework to compare scale and function.
assessment_items.question_text: J.R.D. Tata founded Tata Airlines in 1932 — India's first airline — and later expanded the Tata Group into steel, cars, power, and chemicals. He was also known for caring about workers' welfare. A local entrepreneur in a small town opens the first internet café, provides free training to new users, and employs four people from the neighbourhood. Which statement best analyses what these two entrepreneurs have in common, despite their difference in scale?

options.label: A
options.text: Both entrepreneurs are identical in function — scale is the only difference and scale does not affect what an entrepreneur does.

options.label: B
options.text: Both identify an unmet need in their context, organise factors of production to address it, take financial risk, and contribute to the welfare of their community — the entrepreneurship functions are the same regardless of scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Only J.R.D. Tata qualifies as an entrepreneur because entrepreneurship requires large capital investment and national impact.

options.label: D
options.text: The local entrepreneur is not an entrepreneur but a self-employed worker, because entrepreneurship means starting a company that is listed on the stock market.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Partially correct but imprecise — scale does affect the complexity and reach of entrepreneurial functions, so claiming it makes no difference at all is an overstatement; the student has grasped similarity but missed that scale matters in degree.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a misconception that entrepreneurship is defined by size of investment or national scope — the student has not absorbed the chapter's function-based definition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses entrepreneurship with stock-market participation — a common misconception that treats formal corporate status as the criterion for entrepreneurship rather than the functions performed.

competency.competency_text: Students collect and organise information about economic institutions and explain their significance.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe government technology platforms such as SWAYAM and the National Career Service portal and explain their significance for human capital development.
assessment_items.question_text: SWAYAM offers free Massive Open Online Courses for learners from Grade 9 upwards in subjects such as robotics, aquaculture, and textile printing. The National Career Service portal connects job seekers to employment opportunities across sectors. Explain the significance of each platform for human capital development in India, and identify one barrier that might prevent a student in a rural area from benefiting from either platform.
expected_elements: Explanation of SWAYAM's significance: it removes geographical barriers to specialised education and skill training, enabling learners anywhere to access courses that were previously available only in cities or institutions.

Explanation of the National Career Service portal's significance: it connects workers to employment opportunities they would not otherwise know about, expanding the effective labour market and enabling better matching of skills to jobs.

Identification of at least one realistic barrier for a rural student — such as lack of reliable internet access, absence of a device, low digital literacy, or electricity supply gaps — tied specifically to the platform's mode of delivery.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who have personal experience with limited connectivity may draw on that experience as their barrier example.

competency.competency_text: Students recognise the geographic distribution of resources and explain its implications for production.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain how the uneven geographic distribution of natural resources influences where and how production is organised.
assessment_items.question_text: Coal is found mainly in Jharkhand and Odisha, fish in coastal states such as Kerala and Andhra Pradesh, and oil in Gujarat and Assam. A steel manufacturer based in Maharashtra needs coal to power its furnaces. Which statement best explains how the geographic distribution of this natural resource affects the manufacturer?

options.label: A
options.text: The manufacturer must either transport coal from Jharkhand or Odisha, adding to costs, or relocate operations closer to the coal-producing regions.

options.label: B
options.text: Geographic distribution has no effect on producers because the government delivers all natural resources to factories free of charge.

options.label: C
options.text: The manufacturer can substitute coal with any other natural resource found locally, since all natural resources serve the same productive function.

options.label: D
options.text: Since coal is a natural resource and therefore classified as 'land', the manufacturer automatically owns all coal deposits in India.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a misunderstanding of how natural resources reach producers — the student has confused public infrastructure or subsidies with free universal delivery, missing the cost and logistics dimension.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reflects a misconception that all natural resources are interchangeable — the student has not understood that specific industries require specific inputs and that substitution is technically constrained.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the economic classification of land (all natural resources) with ownership rights — classifying something as 'land' in economics does not confer ownership; it identifies the factor category.

competency.competency_text: Students recognise the geographic distribution of resources and explain its implications for production.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse how the geographic dispersal of inputs across a supply chain creates both productive capacity and vulnerability to disruption.
assessment_items.question_text: India's mobile phone manufacturers source semiconductor chips from East Asia, lithium from South America, and glass from domestic suppliers. During the COVID-19 pandemic, international borders closed and shipping was disrupted. Which statement best analyses how the geographic dispersal of these inputs affected Indian mobile phone production?

options.label: A
options.text: Geographic dispersal had no effect because domestic glass suppliers could substitute for all the missing imported components.

options.label: B
options.text: Dispersal across distant regions gave manufacturers access to specialised inputs in normal times but created vulnerability when international supply routes were disrupted — showing that geographic spread is both an advantage and a risk.

options.label: C
options.text: The disruption was caused entirely by poor entrepreneurship decisions, not by the geographic spread of inputs.

options.label: D
options.text: Production was unaffected because technology allows manufacturers to produce semiconductor chips digitally without physical supply chains.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misunderstanding of input specificity — the student has not grasped that different components serve different technical functions and cannot be freely substituted across categories.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misattributes a structural supply chain vulnerability to a single factor (entrepreneurship) — indicates the student has not understood the systemic nature of geographic dispersal risk.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reflects a confusion between digital technology and physical manufacturing — the student has conflated software or digital platforms with the physical supply of hardware components.

competency.competency_text: Students know and appreciate India's historical contributions to knowledge, skill, and cultural heritage.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret evidence from ancient Indian skill traditions to explain how knowledge was organised, transmitted, and applied in production.
assessment_items.question_text: Ancient Indian shipbuilders stitched wooden planks together using cords rather than nails, producing ships that were flexible rather than rigid. These ships successfully navigated the Indian Ocean for over 2,000 years and supported extensive maritime trade. The design guidelines for this and other crafts were recorded in texts called the shilpa shastras and transmitted across generations. Which statement best interprets what this evidence tells us about how knowledge was organised in ancient India?

options.label: A
options.text: Ancient Indian knowledge was primitive because it relied on natural materials like cords instead of using metal nails, which would have been stronger.

options.label: B
options.text: The combination of written design guidelines (shilpa shastras) and practised technique shows that ancient India had a systematic, multigenerational approach to organising and preserving production knowledge.

options.label: C
options.text: The stitched shipbuilding technique was accidental — it was adopted because metal nails had not yet been invented in India at that time.

options.label: D
options.text: Since these techniques have declined, they were not actually useful and were simply replaced by more efficient foreign methods that Indian craftspeople preferred.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a presentist bias — the student is judging ancient materials by modern standards without considering the engineering rationale (flexibility for ocean navigation) that made the cord technique superior for its purpose.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads a deliberate engineering choice as an accidental or default outcome — the student has missed the chapter's point that the technique was chosen for specific performance reasons related to Indian Ocean conditions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Conflates the decline of a technique with its ineffectiveness — the student has not distinguished between historical success and later displacement, which the chapter attributes to specific socio-economic pressures, not technical failure.

competency.competency_text: Students know and appreciate India's historical contributions to knowledge, skill, and cultural heritage.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret evidence from ancient Indian skill traditions to explain how knowledge was organised, transmitted, and applied in production.
assessment_items.question_text: In ancient India, work was considered an offering requiring devotion, blending kalā (art) and vidyā (knowledge). Tools were worshipped in a tradition that continues today as Vishwakarma Puja or Ayudha Puja. The shilpa shastras contained detailed design guidelines for sculptures, paintings, buildings, wooden items, and jewellery. What does the combination of this cultural practice and this textual tradition suggest about the relationship between skill and knowledge in ancient Indian production?

options.label: A
options.text: Skill and knowledge were kept entirely separate — artisans worked with their hands while scholars wrote the texts, and the two groups never interacted.

options.label: B
options.text: The worship of tools and the codification of design guidelines in texts together show that ancient Indian production integrated artistic skill, technical knowledge, and cultural meaning into a unified practice.

options.label: C
options.text: The shilpa shastras were religious texts unrelated to actual production — craftspeople learned their skills entirely by trial and error without consulting any written sources.

options.label: D
options.text: Tool worship replaced the need for formal training — once tools were blessed, craftspeople could produce high-quality goods without needing technical knowledge.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students from communities that practise Vishwakarma Puja or Ayudha Puja may draw on that experience to enrich their interpretation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Imposes a false division between theory and practice — the student has missed the chapter's explicit point that kalā and vidyā were blended, not separated, in ancient Indian craft traditions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misclassifies the shilpa shastras as purely religious by disregarding their content (design guidelines for sculptures, buildings, jewellery) — the student has not engaged with what the texts actually contain.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reduces a cultural practice (tool worship) to a magical substitute for knowledge — the student has not understood that the worship expressed devotion to craft skill rather than replacing it.
